Text: The ClassLoader Subsystem linked resolution step replaces {{c1::symbolic references}} in the runtime constant pool with {{c2::direct references}} to memory.
Extra: This dynamic linking step is optional and can happen either lazily (at runtime use) or eagerly during class verification.

Text: During the linking preparation step, static variables are initialized to their {{c1::default values}}, whereas their explicit programmer values are assigned in the {{c2::initialization}} phase.
Extra: For instance, a static integer variable initialized to five gets value zero in Preparation and five in Initialization.

Text: The JIT compiler optimizes hot paths by using {{c1::C1 Client}} compiler for rapid compilation with light profiling, and {{c2::C2 Server}} compiler for aggressive optimizations.
Extra: C1 provides fast startup and early execution speed, while C2 maximizes total throughput for long-running production server processes.

Text: JIT compilation hot-spot profiling relies on {{c1::method invocation counters}} and {{c2::back-edge counters}} to track execution frequencies.
Extra: Method counters track calls to methods, while back-edge counters track iterations of loops to identify potential candidate code for JIT compiling.

Text: The Young Generation is partitioned into three main zones: one {{c1::Eden}} space and two {{c2::Survivor}} spaces (S0 and S1).
Extra: All new objects are allocated in Eden, and are copied back and forth between S0 and S1 during Minor GC cycles.

Text: According to the {{c1::weak generational hypothesis}}, most allocated Java objects die young, which justifies separating heap memory into Young and Old generations.
Extra: This hypothesis allows garbage collectors to run very fast Minor GCs only on the Young Generation, ignoring the older, larger gen.

Text: Shenandoah GC concurrent compaction uses {{c1::Brooks Pointers}} or load barriers to dynamically redirect application threads reading or writing to objects in transit.
Extra: Compare-And-Swap (CAS) operations modify this pointer value to atomicly swap the reference from the old object to the new copied object.

Text: Standard JVM options are stable, while non-standard options begin with the prefix {{c1::`-X`}}, and experimental options begin with the prefix {{c2::`-XX`}}.
Extra: Experimental `-XX` flags require diagnostic/experimental flags to be unlocked before they are accepted by the JVM launcher in production.

Text: The JVM flag {{c1::`-Xms`}} sets the initial Java heap size, while the flag {{c2::`-Xmx`}} sets the maximum Java heap size.
Extra: Setting these equal to each other avoids dynamic heap resizing pause overhead in production environments, saving CPU cycles.

Text: The flag `-XX:NewRatio=3` configures the size ratio of the Old Generation to the Young Generation to be {{c1::3::ratio number}}, meaning Old Gen is 3/4 of the total heap.
Extra: The Young Generation takes up the remaining one fourth of the heap space under this configuration in HotSpot.

Text: A {{c1::thread dump}} is a snapshot of all active thread execution paths and states, while a {{c2::heap dump}} is a binary snapshot of all objects allocated in memory.
Extra: Thread dumps diagnose deadlocks and execution halts, whereas heap dumps analyze memory leaks and object retention issues.

Text: To capture a thread dump on a Linux system programmatically, one can use the {{c1::`jstack`}} CLI utility, whereas {{c2::`jmap`}} is used to capture heap dumps.
Extra: The process ID (PID) of the target JVM must be provided as an argument to these command line utilities.
